bib.title: Llama2Vec: Unsupervised Adaptation of Large Language Models for Dense Retrieval

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Llama2Vec: Unsupervised Adaptation of Large Language Models for Dense Retrieval" (the LLaRA / Llama2Vec paper; arXiv 2312.15503v2, revised 23 Nov 2025). Authors: Zheng Liu, Chaofan Li, Shitao Xiao, Yingxia Shao, Defu Lian (BUPT, BAAI, USTC, PolyU). The text has no venue line, so treat it as a preprint, 2023 (v2 2025). The source file is named liu-2023-llama2vec.pdf.

COVERAGE: 46194 of 46194 chars read, all 11 pages, including the references. No appendix exists; the results are in Tables 1-7 in the body. Extraction was clean. The tables came out as text rows and I read them as printed. The figures were not rendered.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Llama2Vec adapts LLaMA-2-7B without labels (continued pre-training) so the final-token embedding captures global sentence meaning. Two tasks do this. EBAE predicts the input sentence's own vocabulary from its embedding. EBAR predicts the next sentence's vocabulary from its embedding.
  number: none (method). 10,000 adaptation steps, batch 256, sequence length 1024, learning rate 1e-5.
  setup: LLaMA-2-7B base, Wikipedia corpus curated by DPR. Fine-tuning follows the RepLLaMA recipe (LoRA, ANN hard negatives, contrastive loss).
  quote: "We perform 10,000 steps of Llama2Vec adaptation in total, with a batch size of 256, a sequence length of 1024, and a learning rate of 1e-5."
  where: p.5 (Sec 4.1)
- claim: On MS MARCO passage retrieval it reaches MRR@10 43.1 and Recall@1000 99.5. That beats the same-backbone RepLLaMA (41.2 and 99.4), OpenAI-Ada-002 (34.4, 98.6) and BM25 (18.4, 85.3). Its NDCG@10 on DL'19 is 73.4, below RepLLaMA's 74.3. The authors blame the small test set.
  number: 43.1 MRR@10; 99.5 R@1000
  setup: MS MARCO dev, 7B model, hard-negative fine-tuning (Table 1).
  quote: "LLaMA2-Llama2Vec 7B hard 43.1 99.5 73.4 72.9" and "it achieves a MRR@10 of 43.1 and a Recall@1000 of 99.5"
  where: Table 1, p.4-5
- claim: Compared with the best BERT-size models fine-tuned with hard negatives, it gains almost 4 points of MRR@10.
  number: ~+4% MRR@10
  setup: vs RetroMAE+hard and SimLM+hard, passage dev.
  quote: "the switch to Llama2Vec brings forth almost +4% gains in MRR@10"
  where: p.5
- claim: On MS MARCO document retrieval it reaches MRR@100 47.9 against RepLLaMA's 45.6 (+2.3) and BM25's 27.7. The authors credit the LLM's long context, which lets documents be encoded whole instead of chunked.
  number: 47.9 MRR@100; R@100 94.1; DL'19 NDCG@10 68.2 vs 65.0 for RepLLaMA
  setup: MS MARCO doc dev (Table 2). The text says it beats the earlier BERT-based methods "by +5.7% point"; the printed table gap to COSTA (42.2) is 5.7.
  quote: "LLaMA2-Llama2Vec 7B hard 47.9 94.1 68.2 63.6" and "Llama2Vec continues to outperform RepLLaMA, with a +2.3% improvement in MRR@100"
  where: Table 2, p.5-6
- claim: Zero-shot on BEIR (trained on MS MARCO only), the average NDCG@10 is 56.4. BM25 scores 42.9, RepLLaMA 53.9, Ada-2 51.4, SGPT 52.1 and GTR-XXL 48.6. It beats BM25 on 13 of 14 datasets and beats RepLLaMA on 12 of 14. The authors say BM25 beat the BERT-style dense models when BEIR launched, and LLM encoders reversed that.
  number: 56.4 avg NDCG@10; 13/14 vs BM25; "31% relatively"
  setup: BEIR, 14 datasets, 7B model fine-tuned on MS MARCO.
  quote: "Llama2Vec outperforms BM25 on 13/14 datasets and goes beyond its average performance by 31% relatively."
  where: Table 3 and p.6
- claim: BM25 still wins on some individual BEIR sets, which matters for the hybrid-search note. SciFact is BM25 67.9 vs Llama2Vec 74.8, so dense wins there. SCIDOCS is 14.1 vs 18.9, dense wins. On the others, dense wins by smaller margins or by a lot. BM25 beats the BERT dense baseline on several sets (e.g. Touche 44.2 vs 25.9, ArguAna 39.7 vs 26.5, T-COVID 59.5 vs 61.5 is close). BM25 beats Llama2Vec only on FEVER-like sets? No: BM25 FEVER is 65.1 vs 81.3, so it loses there too. The one set where BM25 comes out ahead of Llama2Vec is not visible in the table; the authors state 13/14, so exactly one set goes to BM25 (not identified in the text, and I could not verify which from the rows).
  number: BM25 avg 42.9
  setup: as above
  quote: "BM25 59.5 61.5 50.1 64.9 81.3 87.3 84.7 86.9" (T-COVID row, BM25 column first)
  where: Table 3, p.5
- claim: The authors' own table shows BM25 beating Llama2Vec on at least one set. Checking the rows: SciFact BM25 67.9 vs 74.8 (dense wins), Touche BM25 44.2 vs 34.2 (BM25 wins). So the 14th set is Touche.
  number: Touche 44.2 (BM25) vs 34.2 (Llama2Vec)
  setup: BEIR zero-shot
  quote: "Touche 44.2 25.9 25.6 29.1 28.0 25.4 30.5 34.2"
  where: Table 3. NOTE: in that row the columns are BM25 44.2, BERT 25.9, GTR 25.6, CPT 29.1, Ada-2 28.0, SGPT 25.4, RepLLaMA 30.5, Llama2Vec 34.2. Read literally, Llama2Vec (34.2) is below BM25 (44.2). This is my reading of the printed table; the text does not name the exception. Treat as a caller-checkable inference, not a stated claim.
- claim: Zero-shot on the LlamaIndex retrieval eval, Llama2Vec scores MRR 70.56 and hit rate 92.31. RepLLaMA scores 68.43 and 91.35, OpenAI text-embedding-3-large 67.37 and 90.38, and bge-m3 69.67 and 88.94. Note that bge-m3 comes from the same group of authors.
  number: 70.56 MRR; 92.31 hit rate
  setup: Table 4, zero-shot; dataset details not given in the text.
  quote: "Llama2Vec 70.56 92.31"
  where: Table 4, p.5-6
- claim: The prompt choice matters. NEXT-SELF (query NEXT, document SELF) is used for correlation tasks like QA. SELF-SELF suits long paraphrase (ArguAna). NEXT-NEXT suits short paraphrase (Quora). Choosing per task (Ada*) gives BEIR avg 57.4, against 56.1 for N2S, 52.3 for N2N, 47.6 for no prompt and 30.2 for S2S.
  number: 57.4 avg (Ada*)
  setup: BEIR, Table 5. Ada* picks the best prompt per dataset by task type.
  quote: "Ada* 57.4 56.5 38.2 45.9 81.3 48.5 70.1 38.2 64.6 88.3 18.9 74.8 34.2 86.9 43.2"
  where: Table 5, p.6-7. Caution: Ada* is 57.4 here, but Table 3 reports 56.4 for Llama2Vec. The paper does not reconcile these; Table 3 matches N2S's per-dataset values rather than Ada*.
- claim: Adaptation raises the lexical overlap between query and answer in the model's vocabulary space. Take the top-N predicted vocab words for each and score them with BM25. The adapted model scores higher than the initial LLaMA-2, and fine-tuning raises it further. The authors link this to query/document expansion (doc2query, GAR), saying it is done implicitly in the embedding.
  number: top-1000: 219.09 initial, 392.80 adapted, 542.89 fine-tuned; top-100: 18.01, 47.68, 84.08
  setup: MS MARCO query/answer pairs, BM25 over predicted vocabularies (Table 6).
  quote: "Top-N Initial Adapt Fine-Tune ... 1000 219.09 392.80 542.89"
  where: Table 6, p.6
- claim: Shrinking the embedding from 4096 dims hurts. Linear projection drops MRR@10 from 43.1 to about 41 at 768 dims. Sparsification (top-N entries) holds up better, at 41.5 for 768 dims and 42.3 for 2048. The authors say this shows a need for light-weight LLM retrievers.
  number: 4096 dims 43.1; 768 dims 41.0 (DimRed) / 41.2 (DimRed*) / 41.5 (Sparse)
  setup: MS MARCO passage dev, Table 7.
  quote: "768 41.0 41.2 41.5" and "both methods suffer from notably performance loss after dim reduction"
  where: Table 7, p.7
- claim: Costs. The joint prompt "input SELF </s> NEXT </s>" with a mask that hides the two suffixes from each other saves almost half the compute of running the input twice.
  number: ~50% compute saving
  quote: "such an operation will save almost 50% of the computation cost compared with the naive method."
  where: p.3

LIMITS
- Authors concede: tested only on a 7B model; English-only; running cost of such large embedding models is a concern (Sec 6).
- No latency, index-size or throughput numbers. The only cost argument is the dimension study. A 4096-dim vector from a 7B model is much heavier than a 768-dim BERT embedding, so this is not a like-for-like comparison with small models.
- No hybrid (BM25 + dense) experiment. BM25 appears only as a baseline, so the paper says nothing about fusion. For a hybrid-search note, the usable points are BM25's 42.9 BEIR average, the Touche case (read from the table) and the authors' statement that LLM encoders overturned the earlier result that BM25 beat dense models zero-shot.
- Fine-tuned on MS MARCO only. No in-domain results for other corpora, and no ablation of EBAE vs EBAR alone in the text.
- The 56.4 (Table 3) vs 57.4 (Table 5 Ada*) mismatch is unexplained.
- Dated: BEIR "state of the art" and OpenAI-Ada-002 / text-embedding-3 comparisons reflect late 2023. Newer embedders likely exceed these numbers (I could not check that from this source).
- Authors are also behind the bge-m3 baseline and the FlagEmbedding code.

BUILDS ON
- RepLLaMA (Ma et al., 2023): same fine-tuning recipe, closest baseline.
- Auto-regressive LLM final-token embeddings (Zhang et al., 2023, "Language models are universal embedders"; Muennighoff 2022, SGPT; Neelakantan et al., 2022).
- LLaMA-2 (Touvron et al., 2023), LoRA (Hu et al., 2021), ANN hard negatives (Xiong et al., 2020, ANCE).
- RetroMAE (Liu and Shao, 2022) and RetroMAE-2 (Liu et al., 2023): the same lead author's reconstruction-style pre-training for BERT-size encoders.
- Sparsification from SPLADE v2 (Formal et al., 2021); doc2query (Nogueira et al., 2019) and GAR (Mao et al., 2020) for the expansion argument; DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020) for the Wikipedia corpus; BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021).

CODE: none. The loss is Eq. 4 (multi-class cross-entropy over target tokens using the LM head W) and Eq. 5 (contrastive loss with query prompted by NEXT, answer by SELF). Prompts: "The input sentence is:" (SELF), "The next sentence is:" (NEXT).

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): EBAE and EBAR prompts on one sentence, showing the inductive and deductive embedding.
- Fig 2 (p.3): the attention mask in which the SELF and NEXT suffixes cannot see each other, so one pass yields both embeddings.
I did not render these.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction of tables is flattened, so column alignment in Table 3 was inferred from the header order. The Table 3 values I rely on (Touche, T-COVID) follow that order, but the "BM25 loses on Touche" reading is mine, not stated by the authors. Tell the note's author to check Table 3 directly before citing that row. The Ada* 57.4 vs Table 3 56.4 mismatch also needs checking. One of my claim bullets (the "BM25 still wins" one) rambled mid-thought; the two bullets after it carry the corrected reading.
